Heat Stable Amine Salts (HSAS) are compounds that form in amine systems when acidic gases like hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) are treated. Over time, these salts accumulate and can damage equipment, reduce the efficiency of the system, and make the amine less effective at removing acidic gases. The document [D1] explains that HSAS are "heat stable," meaning they remain in the amine solution even when heated, which complicates their removal. 

Why would anyone add caustic (like NaOH) to the amine? The goal is to neutralize the HSAS by reacting with them, preventing corrosion and maintaining system performance. However, adding too much caustic can over-neutralize the amine, which reduces its ability to absorb acidic gases. ⟦removed⟧
